taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO accepted species concept. Historical Verbena combinations remain useful search aliases in sources. Source-pool nominate variety is represented in this species-level learner card; no separate variety card created.
look_here_first: LOOK AT THE MATURE LEAVES BEFORE THE FLOWERS. They occur in OPPOSITE pairs on a slightly 4-angled, hairy stem, and the larger leaves are deeply cut twice into many fernlike narrow lobes. Then inspect the tight terminal cluster: five-lobed, two-lipped tubular lilac-to-purple flowers with a bract beneath EACH flower. From the side look for the narrow pointed flower bract near/slightly longer than its hairy 5-toothed calyx, and later for a fruiting spike that stretches out so the persistent calyces become more separated. Compare with Glandularia pumila (smaller, broadly divided leaves and shorter compact fruiting spike) before confirming. Purple flowers alone never prove this ID.

project_inclusion.range_basis: South-central Texas floristic voucher set explicitly records G. bipinnatifida in Uvalde, Medina, and Real counties; Williamson and Travis are also independently documented.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Exact county voucher evidence; no inferred counties.

best_field_traits: OPPOSITE leaves at hairy, often four-angled stem nodes; follow a stem and check pairs.
Mature leaf often deeply twice-pinnately cut, with many secondary narrow lobes, fern-like at a glance.
Low mat-forming to ascending habit on sunny, open Central Texas prairie/limestone edges.
Rounded terminal cluster is a SHORT DENSE SPIKE, not a true single composite flower.
Each corolla is a fused tube ending in five unequal lobes (two upper/three lower).
Hairy persistent five-toothed calyx; a separate narrow bract subtends each flower, often slightly longer.
After bloom, the spike axis lengthens so calyces become spaced; compare with G. pumila.
Size, color and lobe count vary: combine mature leaf, bract/calyx and spike, never purple flowers alone.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: G. pumila is lower and more compact, with smaller broadly ovate leaves divided into fewer broader lobes and a very short dense spike that does not elongate much in fruit. G. bipinnatifida looks more finely cut and feathery.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Opposite and decussate on 4-angled stems; petiolate, larger leaves often broad triangular in overall outline.
morphology_keys.leaf_dissected: Larger mature leaves opposite, petiolate, often broadly triangular/ovate in overall outline and deeply once- or twice-pinnately divided: each primary lobe often has secondary sublobes, creating a fernlike effect. Smaller apical/young leaves may be less divided. Examine mature mid-stem leaves and photograph both sides.
morphology_keys.flowering_structure: Dense terminal spike, flat-to-rounded in flower; spike rachis extends conspicuously as fruits mature, and individual flowers/bracts can become spaced.
morphology_keys.fruit: Flowering spike axis elongates as seeds develop, separating the hairy persistent calyces; inside each mature calyx the schizocarp yields four one-seeded mericarps (nutlets). A dense *flowering* head and elongated *fruiting* spike can occur on the same plant.
field_checks: Compare mature leaves at same scale, not small juvenile leaves.
Inspect older fruiting head for elongation and separated calyces.
Check single calyx/flower tube in profile for supporting measures.
morphology_keys.habitat_habit: Low spreading or ascending, short-lived perennial or annual herb on open limestone, clay/caliche or grassy prairie margins; several stems from base; lower stems may root where they touch soil. Not a cultivar identity.
morphology_keys.stem_nodes: Stem hairy, roughly 4-angled/square in cross-section; leaf pairs opposite/decussate. Angles can be reddish. Supporting family trait; NOT species-specific.
morphology_keys.flower_anatomy: Not five separate petals: the corolla is ONE fused tube ending in five unequal spreading lobes, organized 2 upper + 3 lower; some lower lobes notched. Round to flat-topped tightly crowded terminal flowering spike, often lilac, pale pink or violet. Flowers about 8–12 mm across in UT regional account; variation across populations.
morphology_keys.calyx_bract: Each tiny flower has a narrow awl/lanceolate green bract subtending a hairy five-toothed calyx; bract generally slightly longer than calyx in Williamson specimens. Do not label a bract unless the separate leaflike structure BELOW an individual calyx is visibly resolved.
crew_checklist: 1. Photo full plant and follow creeping/ascending stems.
2. Take TOP-DOWN view of an entire mature opposite LEAF PAIR and one large twice-cut leaf.
3. Photograph a node from the side: leaf pair, stem hair and four-angled stem.
4. Shoot a flower HEAD top-on with the individual fused tubular 5-lobed corollas visible.
5. Shoot SIDE of head at macro scale: find one bract BELOW one hairy calyx, not a random other lobe.
6. Shoot an old fruiting spike and compare its length to a young flowering one on same plant.

comparisons.key_distinctions: vs LOCAL G. pumila: G. bipinnatifida usually has larger fernlike twice-cut mature leaves and a more elongating fruiting spike; G. pumila typically smaller broadly divided leaves, very small flowers, compact fruiting spike. Flower color overlaps. vs G. quadrangulata: small pale flowers (often white/lavender), smaller heads and less extensive second-order lobing; county occurrence not assumed. Both Glandularia and Verbena may have opposite leaves, but many Verbena have elongated slender spikes even when flowering. Check leaf + flower bract/calyx + fruit spike as combined ID.

cross_genus_lookalikes.difference: Both can show divided leaves; Glandularia bipinnatifida more typically has compact flower heads at anthesis and conspicuous 1–2-pinnate foliage, while V. halei has slender, often open spikes and lower leaves variably dissected.
Both may have lobed leaves; Gulf vervain usually has coarser, predominantly 3-lobed leaves and elongate spikes, not feathery twice-divided foliage and terminal clustered Glandularia flower heads.
Introduced tall/wiry upright vervain with slender long branching flowering spikes and coarsely toothed, not finely twice-cut foliage; do not equate every purple verbena with native prairie verbena.

Showier rose vervain is more eastern/sandy; mature leaves less deeply dissected and commonly longer corolla tubes; glandular calyx pubescence useful. Not automatically a confirmed Hays-county look-alike.
Escaped/cultivated multi-colored hybrids may have similar clusters; origin and vegetative morphology vary. Do not use nursery cultivar photographs as wild native reference.

crew_key: Opposite hairy leaves on low spreading stems? Inspect a mature mid-stem leaf.
Strong 1–2-stage fernlike incisions? Candidate G. bipinnatifida; shallow fan-lobed leaves suggest G. pumila.
Flower is 5 LOBES on a fused tube, in a rounded terminal crowd of separate little flowers.
Side macro: pointed individual flower bract, hairy five-toothed calyx; confirm real structures, don't assume.
Old fruiting spike elongated and calyces separated? Supports bipinnatifida over often compact G. pumila.
If only purple flower-head photo is available, keep Glandularia sp.; do not promise species.

items.label: Mature leaves & flowers
items.image_role: Field close view — one five-lobed flower and a deeply cut single leaf on the same Texas plant
items.caption: Five lobes belong to one fused corolla, not five separate petals. Lower right shows one deeply incised simple leaf, not a set of separate leaflets.

items.label: Comal County flower structure
items.image_role: Five lobes of the fused tubular corolla and multiple densely hairy developing floral calyces
items.caption: One individually identifiable purple five-lobed corolla at upper center; multiple green hairy closed floral units beneath, not a single bract or a ripe seed head.
items.why_it_matters: Local Comal County flower detail; purple shade and flower size alone are not enough to separate other Glandularia.

items.label: Bristly stem and flower

items.label: Hairy terminal flowering spike
items.image_role: Hairy persistent green floral structures immediately below the purple flowers, natural dry-prairie habit

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Prairie verbena: leaves first, not just purple blooms
steps: Look for one deeply divided SIMPLE leaf (not many separate leaflets) and an opposite leaf pair at a node.
Find one complete flower: five uneven lobes on one fused tubular corolla.
Follow the densely hairy terminal spike and look for an old fruiting spike that elongates.
Before naming it, compare G. pumila's smaller, more broadly lobed leaves and compact fruiting spike.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Mature leaf dissection + terminal tubular corolla head + fruiting-spike behavior is a stronger ID than flower color or an isolated flower.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Bract vs calyx on a SINGLE flower, a measured calyx profile and old elongated fruiting head are not yet demonstrated in these photographs. Do not claim those structures were arrow-verified.
